name: avahi
desc: Service Discovery for Linux using mDNS/DNS-SD
why: Avahi is a door into mDNS and DNS-SD, protocols running silently on most networks that few people ever inspect.

brief.what_it_is: Avahi is a free, LGPL implementation of DNS-SD (RFC 6763) over multicast DNS (mDNS, RFC 6762) that runs on Linux and is compatible with Apple Bonjour/Zeroconf. It takes service announcements and hostname queries from the local network and makes them visible to the machine: you can browse who is offering printers, chat or file shares, and resolve .local names. Its main outputs are a system daemon, a D-Bus API, and command-line tools such as avahi-browse and avahi-publish. Services can also be published with XML files in /etc/avahi/services.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it lets you plug a laptop into a network and instantly see other people to chat with, printers to print to, and shared files, as Apple's Bonjour does on macOS. It is primarily aimed at Linux systems and ships by default in most distributions.
brief.how_it_works: A daemon, avahi-daemon, takes part in mDNS and DNS-SD on the local network and exposes its state over D-Bus, which is the primary API for most uses. Services can alternatively be published by dropping an XML service definition into /etc/avahi/services. A companion project, nss-mdns, hooks into nsswitch so that *.local hostname lookups work in all system programs.

brief.install_notes: The package metadata lists twelve executables, including avahi-autoipd, avahi-browse-domains, avahi-dnsconfd, avahi-publish-address and avahi-resolve-address. The primary API is D-Bus, which the README says is required for most of Avahi's usage. Publishing services can be done without D-Bus by placing XML files in /etc/avahi/services. For *.local name resolution in ordinary programs, the separate nss-mdns project is needed. I did not find build or configuration steps in the pages I read.
brief.standout: Avahi is a plain, open implementation of the same discovery protocols Apple markets as Bonjour, and it is already in most Linux distributions, so the network chatter most people never inspect can be seen and used with ordinary tools. Services can be advertised with a static XML file, with no code.
brief.status: Quiet but present. The latest release on the homepage is Avahi 0.8, dated 2020-02-18. The most recent news is from December 2023, when the repositories moved to a new GitHub organisation and the website moved to GitHub Pages. The GitHub README cites a copyright range through 2022 and lists active coverage, fuzzing and codespell reports. I could not find a release date for the current master branch.
brief.caveats: Primarily for Linux. The homepage says it is not ported to Windows and will run on many other BSD-like systems. The primary API is D-Bus, so some uses need a running system bus. The homepage's download index at /download/ was reported broken in December 2023. The README does not include usage examples, so the command details here come only from the executable list.

entry.title: Avahi
entry.tldr: Avahi is the Linux implementation of mDNS and DNS-SD, the Bonjour-style protocols that let machines announce and find printers, shares and .local names.
entry.deeper_look:
Avahi is a free, LGPL implementation of DNS Service Discovery (RFC 6763) over Multicast DNS (RFC 6762). It is compatible with Apple Bonjour and aimed mainly at Linux. A daemon, avahi-daemon, listens to the local network, hears what other machines announce, and makes it visible to programs on your machine. It also announces what your machine offers.

The homepage describes the goal as plugging a laptop into a network and instantly seeing other people to chat with, printers to print to, and shared files, the way Bonjour does on macOS. It ships by default in most Linux distributions, so it is probably already running on a Linux machine near you.

The idea underneath is that discovery needs no central server. Hosts ask questions to a multicast address and answer for themselves. That is why `.local` names and "find a printer" menus work on a home network with no configuration. Avahi exposes this through D-Bus, which is its primary API, and through a set of command-line tools such as avahi-browse and avahi-publish-service.

You can also advertise a service with no code at all: drop an XML service definition into /etc/avahi/services. For `.local` lookups to work in ordinary programs, the separate nss-mdns project hooks into nsswitch.
entry.install:
brew install avahi
# Needs D-Bus for most uses. Linux is the primary target; the formula depends on systemd. For .local lookups in ordinary programs, the separate nss-mdns project is also needed.
